analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent bigger tax deductions for corporations' foreign and export profits.
analysis.headline: A bill to permanently extend lower tax rates on multinationals' foreign profits has sat untouched in the House Ways and Means Committee since February 2025, with 7 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2017 tax law, US corporations pay a reduced tax rate on profits from intellectual property — both profits earned abroad and export income tied to US-based patents and software. Those reduced rates are scheduled to shrink after 2025. This bill would cancel that scheduled shrink and lock the lower rates in permanently. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Large US multinational corporations — especially pharmaceutical, software, and technology companies whose profits flow from patents and other intangible property held abroad, and US exporters earning income tied to US-based intangibles. They would keep paying the lower rates permanently instead of seeing their deductions cut in half starting in 2026.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Multinationals holding foreign patents and IP

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes permanent the current deductions equal to 37.5% of foreign-derived intangible income and 50% of GILTI (profits from foreign subsidiaries), which current law is scheduled to reduce to 21.875% and 37.5% for tax years beginning in 2026.
The change would apply for tax years beginning in 2026, so corporations would avoid the scheduled tax increase on that income.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dollar of the permanent deduction is revenue the government forgoes, which must be made up by future borrowing, cuts elsewhere, or other taxes. The scheduled 2026 reduction was the mechanism the 2017 tax law used to phase in higher collection on this income over time.

drawbacks.text: Making the lower rates permanent repeals a scheduled revenue increase, permanently reducing federal income from corporate profits earned abroad or from US-held intangibles — the opposite of what current law would otherwise do starting in 2026.

The benefit is concentrated: only corporations with substantial intangible income — a small set of very large multinationals — claim these deductions, so the cost is spread across all taxpayers while the gain is narrowly held.
An honest supporter would acknowledge there is no new revenue source in the bill; the permanence simply removes the step-down that was part of the original tax law's design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside case is that lower, stable rates on foreign and export income keep investment and headquarters in the US. But the bill's direct effect is a permanent revenue loss that flows to a narrow group of large multinationals, paid for by everyone else through a larger deficit. There is nothing in the bill that offsets the lost revenue, and the scheduled reduction it repeals was the built-in mechanism for the original tax law to raise more revenue over time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Feenstra introduced the bill on February 6, 2025, joined by Rep. Joseph Morelle, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Seven members cosponsored it: 6 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
The action history shows no further steps — no markup, no floor vote, no Senate companion — as of the latest record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one's position has changed. The scheduled reduction in the deductions remains in current law, so the government still expects that revenue in 2026 unless Congress acts separately, while the multinationals the bill would benefit have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill just sat

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan but thin: the bill was introduced by a Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, and the cosponsor list totals 6 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

industries.note: These firms claim the GILTI and foreign-derived intangible income deductions on profits from patents and software held abroad, so permanence locks in their lower tax rate. The gain comes from revenue the Treasury forgoes, which ordinary taxpayers bear. [S2]

industries.industry: US multinationals generally (any domestic corporation with foreign intangible income)
industries.note: The bill applies to all domestic corporations with foreign-derived intangible income or GILTI, not just tech and pharma, and its cost is a permanent reduction in federal revenue. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action ten months after referral and only 7 cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to move on its own. Permanence for these deductions is the kind of provision that typically advances only when folded into a much larger tax package; unless that happens, the bill will sit in Ways and Means until the Congress ends.
